title: Novus Battery Systems: IFRS vs U.S. GAAP for research and development costs
participant_role: International accounting consultant helping Novus Battery Systems explain its IFRS results to U.S. investors
judge_role: Chair of the audit committee of Novus Battery Systems, a Korean company that reports under IFRS

difficulty.rationale: The rules are given in an exhibit, so the student applies them to split $1,000,000 of spending, quantifies a $600,000 difference and explains standard setters and comparability; the reasoning and judge questions keep it at ICDC level.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of an international accounting consultant working with NOVUS BATTERY SYSTEMS, a company headquartered in Seoul, South Korea, that designs batteries for electric vehicles. The chair of the audit committee (judge) has asked you to explain how Novus's accounting for research and development compares with U.S. accounting.

Novus prepares its financial statements under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). U.S. investors and analysts want to compare Novus with its main U.S. competitor, which reports under U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP).

This year, Novus spent $1,000,000 developing a new solid-state battery cell. The research phase cost $400,000 for early laboratory testing of new materials and cell designs. The development phase cost $600,000 for building and testing prototypes, and all of it was spent after all of the IFRS conditions for development costs shown in the rules summary had been met. Commercial production of the new cell is scheduled to begin next year.

The chair (judge) has heard that the two frameworks give different profit figures for the same spending and wants to know why, who makes these rules, and how investors should compare the two companies.

[Research and development spending and rules summary: see exhibits]

You must:
- Apply the IFRS and U.S. GAAP rules to Novus's $1,000,000 of research and development costs
- Calculate the effect of each framework on current-year pre-tax income and total assets
- Explain who sets IFRS and U.S. GAAP, including the SEC's role for U.S. companies, and why the two sets of standards differ
- Advise how an investor should compare Novus with its U.S. competitor

You will present the information to the audit committee chair (judge) in a role-play to take place in the board room. The audit committee chair (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the audit committee chair's (judge's) questions, the audit committee chair (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Doesn't capitalizing make our profit look fake?
Which approach gives investors a truer picture?

solution.overview: A strong answer applies the rules summary: IFRS expenses the $400,000 of research and capitalizes the $600,000 of development as an intangible asset, while U.S. GAAP expenses all $1,000,000, so IFRS pre-tax income and total assets are $600,000 higher this year. The presenter explains that the IASB sets IFRS, the FASB sets U.S. GAAP and the SEC oversees reporting by U.S. public companies, that the frameworks differ in how much judgment they allow, and advises investors to put both companies on the same basis before comparing.

answer: IFRS: research is expensed, so $400,000 is expensed
IFRS: the development conditions were met, so the $600,000 is capitalized as an intangible asset
The asset is amortized once it is available for use (next year, when production starts)
U.S. GAAP: all $1,000,000 is expensed as incurred
R&D expense: IFRS $400,000 vs U.S. GAAP $1,000,000
Current-year pre-tax income is $600,000 higher under IFRS
Total assets are $600,000 higher under IFRS (the capitalized development costs)
In later years IFRS shows amortization expense that U.S. GAAP does not, so the gap narrows over time

by_task.task: Standard setters and why the rules differ
answer: The IASB, an independent international board, issues IFRS, used in more than 140 jurisdictions including Korea
The FASB, a private U.S. board, issues U.S. GAAP
The SEC has legal authority over financial reporting by U.S. public companies and recognizes the FASB's standards as U.S. GAAP
IFRS is more principles based and allows judgment to show development as a resource; U.S. GAAP chooses one conservative, uniform rule because R&D benefits are uncertain

by_task.task: Comparing Novus with the U.S. competitor
answer: Put both on the same basis: expense Novus's $600,000 of capitalized development to compare with the competitor's U.S. GAAP figures
Read the accounting policy notes in each company's annual report
Compare cash spent on R&D, which is the same under both frameworks
Novus can help by disclosing capitalized development costs clearly and showing key figures on a U.S. GAAP basis in investor materials

judge_question_answers.question: Doesn't capitalizing make our profit look fake?
answer: No: it follows IFRS, and the cost is not hidden, it is expensed through amortization over the years the battery earns revenue
Total expense over the project's life is $1,000,000 under both frameworks; only the timing differs
The strict conditions, auditors and note disclosures limit abuse
Investors should still know that this year's profit is $600,000 higher because of that choice

judge_question_answers.question: Which approach gives investors a truer picture?
answer: Neither is simply right; each trades off relevance and reliability
IFRS better matches costs with future revenue and shows the development work as an asset
U.S. GAAP is more conservative and objective and makes U.S. companies easy to compare with each other
For comparing Novus with the U.S. competitor, the truer picture comes from putting both on the same basis

key_concepts.definition: International Financial Reporting Standards, issued by the IASB and used by companies in more than 140 jurisdictions, including listed companies in South Korea.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles set by the FASB; required for U.S. companies that file with the SEC.
The IFRS standard that requires research costs to be expensed and development costs to be capitalized once specific criteria (such as technical feasibility and probable future benefits) are met.
The U.S. GAAP topic that requires research and development costs to be expensed as incurred.
Capitalizing records a cost as an asset to be expensed over future periods; expensing records it as a cost of the current period.
Spreading the cost of an intangible asset over its useful life, starting when the asset is available for use.
The IASB sets IFRS, the FASB sets U.S. GAAP, and the SEC has legal authority over financial reporting by U.S. public companies.
When in doubt, choose the treatment that does not overstate assets or income, such as expensing uncertain R&D.
The quality that lets users compare companies or periods; it requires the same accounting basis or clear adjustments.
Record expenses in the same period as the revenue they help earn, the idea behind amortizing capitalized development costs.

notes: A physical battery cell keeps ASC 730 clearly applicable (software to be sold follows different U.S. GAAP rules). The rules summary exhibit gives students the IAS 38 and ASC 730 rules, so the event tests application and explanation rather than memorization. Korean listed companies use K-IFRS, which is aligned with IASB IFRS. Watch for students who expense the development costs under IFRS, who say total expense differs over the project's life, or who cannot name who sets each set of standards.

items.label: Compare U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) and International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS)

criteria.exceeds: Explains that IFRS (IAS 38) expenses the $400,000 of research and capitalizes the $600,000 of development because all conditions were met, while U.S. GAAP (ASC 730) expenses all $1,000,000, and adds that the capitalized asset is amortized starting next year when production begins, so the gap narrows over time.
criteria.meets: Correctly states that IFRS expenses $400,000 and capitalizes $600,000, while U.S. GAAP expenses the full $1,000,000.
criteria.below: Knows the frameworks differ but expenses the development costs under IFRS, or capitalizes the research costs.
criteria.little: Does not compare the frameworks, or says they treat R&D the same way.

items.label: Explain the nature of accounting standards

criteria.exceeds: Explains that IFRS is more principles based and allows judgment to show development work as a resource (matching costs with future revenue), while U.S. GAAP uses one conservative, uniform rule because R&D benefits are uncertain, and that each trades off relevance against reliability.
criteria.meets: Explains that the standards differ because IFRS allows more judgment while U.S. GAAP is more conservative about uncertain R&D benefits.
criteria.below: Mentions conservatism or judgment in general terms without tying it to the R&D difference.
criteria.little: Does not explain why accounting standards exist or differ.

items.label: Discuss the levels and types of external financial reporting

criteria.exceeds: Advises investors to put both companies on the same basis (expense Novus's $600,000 of capitalized development), read the accounting policy notes, compare cash spent on R&D, and suggests Novus disclose capitalized development clearly and show key figures on a U.S. GAAP basis in investor materials.
criteria.meets: Advises investors to adjust Novus's figures to the same basis as the U.S. competitor and to read the notes in each annual report.
criteria.below: Says the companies are hard to compare but gives no practical way to adjust the numbers.
criteria.little: Gives no advice on comparing the companies, or compares the reported profits directly.

items.label: Discuss the roles and responsibilities of accounting-standards-setting bodies

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the IASB, an independent international board, issues IFRS used in more than 140 jurisdictions including Korea, the FASB, a private U.S. board, issues U.S. GAAP, and the SEC has legal authority over reporting by U.S. public companies and recognizes the FASB's standards as U.S. GAAP.
criteria.meets: Correctly names the IASB as the setter of IFRS, the FASB as the setter of U.S. GAAP, and the SEC as the government body overseeing U.S. public company reporting.
criteria.below: Names only one body correctly, or mixes up the roles, such as saying the SEC writes IFRS.
criteria.little: Cannot name who sets either set of standards.

criteria.exceeds: Shows R&D expense of $400,000 (IFRS) against $1,000,000 (U.S. GAAP), so pre-tax income and total assets are $600,000 higher under IFRS this year, gives the IFRS entry (debit R&D Expense $400,000 and Development Costs $600,000, credit Cash $1,000,000), and explains later amortization narrows the gap.
criteria.meets: Calculates that current-year pre-tax income and total assets are $600,000 higher under IFRS.
criteria.below: Identifies the income difference but not the asset difference, or uses the wrong amount such as $400,000.
criteria.little: Does not quantify any effect on income or assets.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the capitalization choice to higher income and assets now, amortization later, and equal total expense of $1,000,000 over the project's life, showing only timing differs.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the rules summary to the $600,000 difference in income and assets.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or claims total expense differs over the project's life.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the chair a clear plan for investor communication: adjust to one basis, compare cash R&D spending, and disclose capitalized development clearly with U.S. GAAP basis figures.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation on how investors should compare Novus with its U.S. competitor.
criteria.below: Gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.

criteria.exceeds: Explains capitalizing versus expensing and the role of each standard setter in plain language the chair can follow, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the rules, the $600,000 effect and the standard setters clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon or acronyms without explanation, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a side by side table of the $1,000,000 under IFRS and U.S. GAAP or another visual that makes the $600,000 gap obvious, and suggests practical ideas for investor materials.
criteria.meets: Organizes the comparison in a way that makes the difference easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: capitalizing is not fake because it follows IFRS, the cost is amortized over the years the battery earns revenue, total expense is $1,000,000 either way, and strict conditions, auditors and disclosures limit abuse; and neither approach is simply truer, since IFRS gives better matching and U.S. GAAP more conservatism, so comparisons need the same basis.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that only the timing of expense differs and that a fair comparison puts both companies on the same basis.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers such as agreeing that capitalizing inflates profit.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or gives incorrect answers.

key_points: IFRS (IAS 38): expense the $400,000 of research and capitalize the $600,000 of development as an intangible asset
U.S. GAAP (ASC 730): expense all $1,000,000 as incurred
This year IFRS pre-tax income and total assets are $600,000 higher; amortization starts next year when production begins
Total expense over the project's life is $1,000,000 under both frameworks; only the timing differs
The IASB sets IFRS, the FASB sets U.S. GAAP, and the SEC oversees reporting by U.S. public companies
IFRS allows more judgment (matching); U.S. GAAP uses one conservative rule because R&D benefits are uncertain
Investors should put both companies on the same basis, read the policy notes and compare cash spent on R&D
